q: A company issues fully paid bonus shares to its shareholders by capitalising a part of its general reserve. In its cash flow statement, this transaction is:

options.A: Shown as a cash inflow from financing activities
options.B: Shown as a cash outflow from financing activities
options.C: Excluded altogether, since no cash moves in the transaction
options.D: Shown as a cash inflow from operating activities

q: In a cash flow statement prepared by the direct method, the section for operating activities is built up primarily from:

options.A: The major classes of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments, such as cash received from customers and cash paid to suppliers and employees
options.B: The net profit of the year, adjusted for non-cash items
options.C: The net change in the working capital during the year alone
options.D: The cash and bank balances appearing in the balance sheet alone

q: The operating profit of an enterprise, before working capital changes, is Rs 4,75,000. During the year, its stock decreased by Rs 38,000, its debtors increased by Rs 52,000, its creditors increased by Rs 27,000 and its outstanding expenses decreased by Rs 11,000. The cash generated from operations, before tax paid, is:
Plant with a book value of Rs 60,000 is sold by an enterprise for Rs 85,000 during the year. In the funds flow statement, the amount shown as a source of funds on account of this sale is:

options.A: Rs 25,000, being the profit on the sale alone
options.B: Rs 85,000, being the entire sale proceeds
options.C: Rs 60,000, being the book value of the plant
options.D: Nil, because the sale of a fixed asset is not a funds transaction

q: Depreciation charged on plant is sometimes loosely spoken of as a source of funds. The correct position in funds flow analysis is that depreciation is:

options.A: A source of funds, like the issue of shares
options.B: An application of funds, like the purchase of assets
options.C: Neither a source nor an application of funds; it is only added back to the profit in computing the funds from operations, being a non-cash charge
options.D: A change in working capital shown in the schedule of changes

q: The current ratio of an enterprise rises from 1.8 : 1 to 2.4 : 1 in a year, while its quick ratio falls from 1.1 : 1 to 0.8 : 1 over the same year. The most likely explanation of this combination of movements is:

options.A: A heavy build-up of inventory, which raises the current assets but is excluded from the quick assets
options.B: A large increase in the cash and bank balances of the enterprise
options.C: A reduction in the stock held by the enterprise
options.D: A fall in the current liabilities without any change in the current assets

q: The current ratio of an enterprise is 2.75 : 1 and its current liabilities are Rs 2,40,000. Its net working capital is:
Over a series of years, the proprietary ratio of an enterprise steadily falls while its total assets remain broadly unchanged. This trend principally indicates that:

options.A: The stake of the proprietors in the total assets is rising
options.B: The enterprise is depending more and more on its own funds
options.C: The short-term liquidity of the enterprise is steadily improving
options.D: A progressively larger share of the assets is being financed by outside funds, leaving a thinner cushion of safety for the creditors

q: The inventory turnover ratio of an enterprise falls from 9 times to 6 times in a year in which its sales have actually increased. The most likely reading of this fall is:

options.A: Inventory is being converted into sales more quickly than before
options.B: The average stock held by the enterprise has been reduced
options.C: Stock is piling up in relation to sales, locking more funds in inventory and pointing to an accumulation of slow-moving items
options.D: Trade debtors are being collected more slowly than before

q: The gross profit ratio of an enterprise remains unchanged over two years, but its net profit ratio falls in the second year. This pattern most likely arises because:

options.A: Expenses below the gross profit line, such as administration, selling and interest costs, have risen as a proportion of sales in the second year
options.B: The cost of goods sold has risen faster than the sales
options.C: The volume of sales has fallen, while all margins have held steady
options.D: A change in the method of valuing stock has raised the cost of goods sold

q: An enterprise holds stock of Rs 2,85,000, trade debtors of Rs 1,95,000, cash and bank balances of Rs 45,000 and prepaid expenses of Rs 25,000, and has no other current assets. Its current liabilities are Rs 2,00,000. Its quick (liquid) ratio is:
The total assets of an enterprise are Rs 16,00,000, its proprietors' funds are Rs 6,40,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 1,60,000. Its debt-equity ratio, taking debt as long-term debt, is:
The trade debtors of an enterprise were Rs 1,30,000 at the beginning of a year and Rs 1,70,000 at its close. Its credit sales during the year were Rs 18,00,000. Its debtors turnover ratio is:

options.A: 13.8 times
options.B: 10.6 times
options.C: 12 times
options.D: 6 times

q: The sales of an enterprise are Rs 28,00,000 and its cost of goods sold is Rs 19,60,000. Its gross profit ratio is:

The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 9,60,000. Its capital employed consists of equity share capital of Rs 20,00,000, reserves of Rs 12,00,000 and long-term loans of Rs 16,00,000. Its Return on Capital Employed is:

The net profit after tax of a company is Rs 11,40,000 and the preference dividend payable is Rs 90,000. The company has 1,50,000 equity shares, and the market price of its share is Rs 105. Its price-earnings (P/E) ratio is:
The credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 14,60,000 and its average trade creditors are Rs 2,00,000. Taking a year of 365 days, its average payment period is:

options.A: 36.5 days
options.B: 73 days
options.C: 50 days
options.D: 25 days

q: Cash flows on account of income tax are dealt with in a cash flow statement prepared under AS-3 by:

options.A: Disclosing the tax paid separately and classifying it as a cash flow from operating activities, unless it can be specifically identified with an investing or a financing activity
options.B: Classifying the tax paid invariably as a cash flow from financing activities
options.C: Classifying the tax paid invariably as a cash flow from investing activities
options.D: Omitting any separate disclosure of the tax paid

q: A funds flow statement of an enterprise shows a comfortable net increase in working capital for a year in which the enterprise in fact faced an acute shortage of cash. This is possible, and it exposes a limitation of the funds flow statement, because the statement:

options.A: Is always prepared incorrectly when the cash balance falls
options.B: Shows the movement of cash in full detail, item by item
options.C: Deals only with transactions settled in cash
options.D: Records only the net change in working capital as a whole, and an increase in working capital may itself consist largely of stock and debtors even while the cash balance falls

q: Just before the close of its financial year, an enterprise with current assets of Rs 5,00,000 and current liabilities of Rs 2,50,000 pays Rs 1,00,000 in cash to its trade creditors. The immediate effect of this payment is that:

options.A: The current ratio falls and the working capital also falls
options.B: The current ratio rises from 2 : 1 to about 2.67 : 1, although the working capital remains unchanged at Rs 2,50,000
options.C: The current ratio remains exactly unchanged
options.D: The working capital rises by Rs 1,00,000

q: The interest coverage ratio of an enterprise declines from 4 times to 1.2 times over two years. The correct reading of this decline is:

options.A: The interest burden of the enterprise has virtually disappeared
options.B: The enterprise has become safer from the lenders' point of view
options.C: The cushion of earnings available for meeting the interest charge has become very thin, so that even a modest fall in earnings may leave the interest unpaid
options.D: The long-term debt of the enterprise has been repaid in full

q: A zonal railway completes several large capital works during a year, sharply raising its capital-at-charge, but the additional earnings from the new assets are expected to build up only gradually. In the initial years, its return on capital-at-charge will most likely:

options.A: Be depressed, because the capital in the denominator has risen ahead of the earnings that the new assets will generate
options.B: Rise sharply, because new assets always earn from the day they are completed
options.C: Remain wholly unaffected by the addition of capital
options.D: Necessarily turn negative in the very first year

q: Under AS-3, the aggregate cash flows arising from the acquisition and the disposal of subsidiaries or other business units are presented in the cash flow statement:

options.A: As a part of the cash flows from operating activities
options.B: Merged with the funds from operations of the year
options.C: As cash flows from financing activities
options.D: Separately, as cash flows from investing activities, net of the cash and cash equivalents acquired or disposed of

q: Outstanding wages of Rs 30,000, shown among the current liabilities at the beginning of the year, are paid in cash during the year. In a funds flow statement, this payment results in:

options.A: An application of funds
options.B: No flow of funds, because the cash (a current asset) and the outstanding wages (a current liability) fall by the same amount, leaving the working capital unchanged
options.C: A source of funds
options.D: A reduction in the funds from operations of the year

q: The creditors turnover ratio of an enterprise rises sharply over a year, with no change in its pattern of purchases. The most likely reading of this rise is:

options.A: The enterprise is paying its suppliers more slowly than before
options.B: The enterprise is enjoying a longer period of credit from its suppliers
options.C: The enterprise is paying its suppliers more quickly than before, thereby giving up a part of the interest-free credit it earlier enjoyed
options.D: The enterprise has stopped purchasing on credit altogether

q: An enterprise reports healthy funds from operations, yet its cash flow statement shows a negative cash flow from operating activities for the same year. The most likely explanation of this position is:

options.A: Funds have been absorbed heavily in building up stock and debtors during the year, so that the investment in working capital more than consumed the funds generated by operations
options.B: Depreciation charged during the year was unusually high
options.C: Fixed assets were sold during the year at a profit
options.D: Shares were issued during the year for cash

q: In the schedule of changes in working capital, an increase in prepaid expenses during the year is treated as:

options.A: A decrease in working capital
options.B: A source of funds in the funds flow statement
options.C: An application of funds in the funds flow statement
options.D: An increase in working capital, prepaid expenses being a current asset, although the amount so locked up will not itself bring in cash

q: Prepaid expenses are excluded from the quick assets in computing the liquid (quick) ratio principally because:

options.A: Their amount is usually too small to matter
options.B: They represent payments made for services yet to be received and cannot be converted back into cash for paying liabilities
options.C: They are a part of the current liabilities of the enterprise
options.D: They are treated as fixed assets in the balance sheet

q: For the same year, the net profit ratio of an enterprise is noticeably higher than its operating profit ratio. This position most likely arises because:

options.A: The operating expenses of the year have been understated
options.B: The cost of goods sold has been overstated
options.C: The enterprise has earned substantial non-operating income, such as profit on the sale of assets or interest on investments, which lifts the net profit above the operating profit
options.D: The sales of the year have been recorded twice

q: Two analysts compute the debt-equity ratio of the same enterprise from the same balance sheet and arrive at materially different figures. The most likely reason for the difference is:

options.A: One analyst has taken debt as long-term debt alone, while the other has taken all outside liabilities, including current liabilities, as debt
options.B: One analyst has made an arithmetical mistake in adding the balance sheet
options.C: One analyst has used the total assets instead of the liabilities
options.D: One analyst has used the sales of the year in place of the capital

q: For a lender judging whether an enterprise can service a proposed loan out of its own operations, the cash flow statement is more directly useful than the profit and loss account alone because it shows:

options.A: The trend of the accounting profit over past years
options.B: The values at which the assets of the enterprise stand in the books
options.C: The dividend history of the enterprise
options.D: The actual cash generated from operating activities, which is what will be available for servicing the debt, as distinct from the accounting profit that includes non-cash charges and accrued items

q: An enterprise makes an operating loss for a year which remains a loss even after the depreciation and the other non-cash charges of the year are added back. In the funds flow statement, the resulting figure is dealt with as:

options.A: A source of funds
options.B: An application of funds, described as funds lost in operations
options.C: An increase in working capital
options.D: An item to be ignored altogether in the statement

q: The return on equity of an enterprise is 22 per cent, while its return on capital employed is 15 per cent and the after-tax cost of its borrowings is 9 per cent. This gap between the return on equity and the return on capital employed is explained by:

options.A: The absence of any borrowing by the enterprise
options.B: Unfavourable financial leverage, under which the equity holders subsidise the lenders
options.C: Favourable financial leverage: the enterprise earns 15 per cent on the total capital while paying only 9 per cent after tax on the borrowed part of it, the surplus accruing to the equity holders
options.D: The payment of dividend on the preference shares of the enterprise

q: The ratios of two enterprises in the same trade differ considerably, although their real efficiency is much the same. A common reason why such an inter-firm comparison of ratios can mislead is that the two enterprises:

options.A: Follow different accounting policies, such as different methods of charging depreciation or of valuing stock, so that the figures underlying the ratios are not strictly comparable
options.B: Carry on business under different trade names
options.C: Get their accounts audited by different firms of auditors
options.D: Maintain their head offices in different cities

q: An enterprise pays instalments under a finance lease for plant taken by it on lease. Under AS-3 / Ind AS 7, the principal portion of these lease payments is classified in the cash flow statement of the lessee as a cash flow from:

options.A: Operating activities
options.B: Investing activities
options.C: No activity, since a lease involves no cash flow
options.D: Financing activities

q: In the funds flow statement of an enterprise, the total of the sources of funds is Rs 9,40,000, while the applications of funds, other than the change in working capital, total Rs 8,10,000. The difference of Rs 1,30,000 represents:

options.A: An additional source of funds omitted from the statement
options.B: A net increase in working capital of Rs 1,30,000, shown as an application of funds so that the two sides of the statement agree
options.C: The funds from operations of the enterprise
options.D: An error in the preparation of the statement

q: The earnings per share of a company rise sharply in a year in which its total profit after tax is virtually unchanged. The most likely explanation of this rise is:

options.A: The sales of the company have doubled during the year
options.B: The company has been exempted from income tax for the year
options.C: The number of equity shares has fallen, for example through a buy-back by the company of its own shares, so that the same profit is spread over fewer shares
options.D: The company has issued fresh preference shares during the year

q: For the stores organisation of a railway, a steadily worsening stores turnover position, with the closing balances of stock rising in relation to the value of the stores issued, indicates at the concept level that:

options.A: An increasing amount of funds is remaining blocked in inventories instead of circulating back through issues
options.B: Issues of stores are rising faster than the receipts of stores
options.C: The stock in the depots is steadily falling
options.D: Suppliers of stores are not being paid in time

q: In connection with its cash flow statement, an enterprise is required to:

options.A: Keep the composition of its cash balance undisclosed
options.B: Disclose the components of cash only when the auditors ask for them
options.C: Reconcile its cash flow statement with the funds flow statement
options.D: Disclose the components of cash and cash equivalents and reconcile the amounts in the cash flow statement with the equivalent items reported in the balance sheet

q: An analyst converts the balance sheets of two enterprises of very different sizes into common-size statements before comparing them. The main advantage he gains from doing so is that:

options.A: The figures of both enterprises become exact to the last rupee
options.B: Each item is expressed as a percentage of the total assets (or the total of the liabilities side), so that the financial structure of the two enterprises can be compared free of the effect of their differing sizes
options.C: No ratios need thereafter be computed for the two enterprises
options.D: The profits of the two enterprises are equalised for comparison

q: A standard cost is best described as:

options.A: The cost actually incurred on a job in the previous accounting period
options.B: A predetermined cost, worked out in advance of production on the basis of specified conditions of operation, with which the actual cost is compared
options.C: An estimate of what a job is expected to cost, prepared informally for quoting a price
options.D: The average of the actual costs of the last three years, adjusted for inflation

q: Standard costing differs from historical (actual) costing mainly in that standard costing:

options.A: Records costs only after the accounts of the year have been closed
options.B: Does away with the need to record actual costs altogether
options.C: Is confined to the ascertainment of the cost of services, and not of products
options.D: Compares the actual cost with a predetermined standard cost for the same output and reports the difference as a variance for control action

q: An attainable (expected) standard is a standard which:

options.A: Can be achieved under efficient operating conditions, after making due allowance for normal wastage, normal idle time and unavoidable losses
options.B: Can be achieved only under the most favourable conditions conceivable, with no allowance for any wastage or idle time
options.C: Is set at the level of the best performance ever recorded in the past, without any change
options.D: Remains unchanged for a long period and serves only as a basis for measuring trends

q: In fixing the standards of material quantity and labour time for a product, the most reliable basis is provided by:

options.A: The judgement of the works manager alone, based on his past experience
options.B: The average consumption and time recorded in the cost sheets of earlier years
options.C: Systematic technical and engineering studies, including work study and time and motion study, conducted under controlled conditions
options.D: The standards reported to be in use in other factories in the same industry

q: A standard cost card for a product shows a standard material cost based on 5 kg of material per unit. This entry on the card states, in respect of material:

options.A: Only the total standard material cost of the month's production
options.B: Both the standard quantity of material allowed per unit and the standard price at which that quantity is valued
options.C: Only the price at which material was last purchased from the supplier
options.D: The quantity of material to be ordered at a time under the purchase budget

q: Standards once set should NOT be revised merely because:

options.A: There has been a permanent change in the design or specification of the product
options.B: There has been a permanent change in the method or process of manufacture
options.C: Wage rates have been permanently revised under a settlement with the workers
options.D: Prices and efficiency have fluctuated temporarily during a single accounting period, the underlying conditions remaining unchanged

q: When the material price variance is isolated at the point of purchase rather than at the point of consumption, the material held in stores is recorded and issued at:

options.A: The standard price, so that the whole price difference is reported in the period of purchase itself
options.B: The actual price paid to the supplier in each case
options.C: The weighted average of the actual prices of all purchases
options.D: The price ruling on the date of issue to production

q: Where a product is made from two or more materials mixed in a definite proportion, the material usage variance is usefully analysed further into:

options.A: Price variance and cost variance
options.B: Expenditure variance and volume variance
options.C: Mix variance and yield variance
options.D: Rate variance and efficiency variance

q: The material sub-usage variance is the part of the usage variance which remains after separating the effect of:

options.A: Paying a price different from the standard price for the material
options.B: Producing an output different from the budgeted output
options.C: Losing time through abnormal idle time in the factory
options.D: Using the materials in proportions different from the standard mix, that is, after separating the mix variance

q: An adverse labour rate variance may properly arise from:

options.A: Workers taking longer than the standard time to complete the work
options.B: Employing a higher proportion of skilled, higher-paid workers than the standard gang composition provides for, or paying overtime premium not provided in the standard rate
options.C: Excess consumption of material by the workers on the job
options.D: Loss of working hours through a breakdown of machinery

q: In computing the labour efficiency variance, the hours to be compared with the standard hours for the actual output are:

options.A: The hours actually worked on productive work, abnormal idle hours being excluded and reported separately as idle time variance
options.B: The total hours paid for, including all abnormal idle hours
options.C: The budgeted hours for the department for the period
options.D: The hours recorded in the attendance register at the factory gate

q: Normal idle time, such as the time lost in setting up machines and in moving from one job to another, is dealt with in standard costing by:

options.A: Reporting it separately as an idle time variance in every period
options.B: Charging it directly to the Costing Profit and Loss Account as a loss
options.C: Taking it into account while setting the standard itself, by building the allowance into the standard time or the standard rate
options.D: Ignoring it altogether in the cost accounts

q: A standard hour, as a measure used in standard costing and overhead absorption, represents:

options.A: The number of workers employed in the factory during one clock hour
options.B: The total clock hours for which the factory remains open in a day
options.C: The wages payable for one hour of work at the standard wage rate
options.D: The quantity of work which should be performed, or output which should be produced, in one hour under standard conditions of performance

q: The standard price of a material is Rs 34 per kg and the actual price paid is Rs 31 per kg. The actual quantity consumed is 1,800 kg. The material price variance is:

options.A: Rs 5,400 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 5,400 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 3,600 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 1,800 (Favourable)

q: For the actual output, the standard quantity of material allowed is 1,250 kg, but 1,400 kg are actually consumed. The standard price is Rs 24 per kg. The material usage variance is:

options.A: Rs 3,600 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 1,800 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 3,600 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 2,400 (Adverse)

q: For the actual output, the standard material cost is 1,000 kg at Rs 15 per kg. The actual consumption is 1,080 kg purchased and used at Rs 16 per kg. The material cost variance is:

options.A: Rs 1,280 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 2,280 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 2,280 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 1,080 (Adverse)

q: The standard wage rate is Rs 65 per hour and the actual rate paid is Rs 70 per hour for 620 actual hours worked. The labour rate variance is:

options.A: Rs 3,100 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 620 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 4,340 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 3,100 (Adverse)

q: For the actual output, the standard labour time allowed is 1,450 hours, while the actual time taken is 1,300 hours. The standard wage rate is Rs 36 per hour. The labour efficiency variance is:

options.A: Rs 5,400 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 5,400 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 3,600 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 1,500 (Favourable)

q: In a factory, 90 hours are lost as abnormal idle time owing to a power failure. The standard wage rate is Rs 55 per hour. The idle time variance is:

options.A: Rs 4,500 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 5,500 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 4,950 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 4,950 (Favourable)

q: The fixed overhead volume variance arises in a period essentially because:

options.A: The fixed overheads actually spent differ from the fixed overheads budgeted for the period
options.B: The wage rates paid to indirect workers differ from the standard rates
options.C: More working days are available in the period than the budget provided for
options.D: The output actually produced differs from the budgeted output, so that the fixed overheads absorbed at the standard rate differ from the budgeted fixed overheads

q: For judging the performance of a departmental manager, variances which are beyond his control should be:

options.A: Charged to his department in the same way as controllable variances
options.B: Identified and reported separately, so that his appraisal rests on the variances he could influence
options.C: Ignored altogether and not reported to higher management
options.D: Set off against the favourable variances of other departments

q: The chief merit of splitting the total variance on the revision of a standard into a planning (revision) variance and an operational variance is that:

options.A: The operational variance then measures performance against the revised standard reflecting current conditions, so managers are not judged against a standard that events have made unrealistic
options.B: The total variance of the period is thereby reduced
options.C: The need for investigating any variance is thereby removed
options.D: The revised standard can then be dispensed with in the following period

q: An adverse variance disclosed by the standard costing system, which on investigation is found to be due to genuine inefficiency in operations, is finally borne by:

options.A: The closing stock of finished goods, by increasing its value
options.B: The work-in-progress account of the following period
options.C: The Costing Profit and Loss Account of the period, and not carried in the value of stocks
options.D: The general reserve of the enterprise

q: Standard costing is difficult to operate satisfactorily, and yields little benefit, in an undertaking where:

options.A: The same standardised products are manufactured continuously in large quantities
options.B: Production consists mainly of non-standard jobs executed to individual customers' specifications, no two jobs being alike
options.C: Output is produced through a continuous process under stable conditions
options.D: The products, methods and prices remain steady over long periods

q: Standards which are set at a level so tight that the workers regard them as impossible to attain are likely to defeat the purpose of standard costing because they:

options.A: Make the computation of variances more accurate
options.B: Discourage and demoralise the staff, who stop making a serious effort to achieve them and lose faith in the system
options.C: Reduce the material consumption of the factory automatically
options.D: Increase the favourable variances reported every period

q: Valuing the stocks of work-in-progress and finished goods at standard cost, instead of at actual cost, benefits the costing system mainly by:

options.A: Simplifying and speeding up the recording and valuation of stocks, the differences from actual cost being dealt with as variances of the period
options.B: Increasing the profit shown by the financial accounts of the period
options.C: Doing away with the physical verification of stocks
options.D: Ensuring that no variance ever arises on material issues

q: For measuring the effect of selling operations on profit, sales variances are preferably computed on the margin (profit) basis rather than on the value (turnover) basis because the margin basis:

options.A: Requires no information about the quantities actually sold
options.B: Shows a larger total variance than the value basis
options.C: Measures directly the difference the selling performance has made to the profit, which the turnover figures by themselves do not show
options.D: Is prescribed by the Companies Act for the annual accounts

q: The standard mix for a batch of 120 kg is: Material P — 72 kg at Rs 20 per kg, Material Q — 48 kg at Rs 35 per kg. The actual mix used for a batch of 120 kg is P — 60 kg and Q — 60 kg. The material mix variance is:

options.A: Rs 180 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 240 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 420 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 180 (Adverse)

q: A process uses 250 kg of input material costing Rs 24 per kg, from which the standard yield is 200 kg of output. The actual yield obtained from the 250 kg of input is 185 kg. The material yield variance is:

options.A: Rs 360 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 450 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 450 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 375 (Adverse)

q: The budgeted production of a factory is 18,000 units and the standard fixed overhead rate is Rs 7 per unit. Actual production is 20,000 units. The fixed overhead volume variance is:

options.A: Rs 14,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 14,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 7,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 2,000 (Favourable)

q: The budgeted working hours of a factory are 15,000 and the actual hours worked are 13,500. The standard fixed overhead absorption rate is Rs 9 per hour. The fixed overhead capacity variance is:

options.A: Rs 13,500 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 12,150 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 13,500 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 1,500 (Adverse)

q: The budgeted fixed overheads of a factory are Rs 2,70,000 for a month budgeted to have 25 working days. The month actually had 27 working days. The fixed overhead calendar variance is:

options.A: Rs 21,600 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 21,600 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 10,800 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 27,000 (Favourable)

q: The standard variable overhead rate is Rs 14 per hour. The standard time for the actual output is 900 hours, but 1,000 hours are actually worked. The variable overhead efficiency variance is:

options.A: Rs 1,400 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 1,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 14,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 1,400 (Adverse)

q: The standard profit margin of a product is Rs 28 per unit and the actual profit margin realised is Rs 24 per unit. The actual quantity sold is 2,600 units. The sales margin price variance is:

options.A: Rs 10,400 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 10,400 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 7,200 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 2,600 (Adverse)

q: The standard cost card of a product shows: material 5 kg at Rs 18 per kg; labour 2.5 hours at Rs 60 per hour; variable overheads at Rs 12 per labour hour; and fixed overheads at Rs 16 per labour hour. The standard cost per unit of the product is:

options.A: Rs 270
options.B: Rs 290
options.C: Rs 310
options.D: Rs 340

q: The fixed overhead efficiency variance measures the part of the volume variance which arises because:

options.A: The fixed overheads actually incurred differ from the budgeted fixed overheads
options.B: The number of working days in the period differs from the budgeted number
options.C: The hours actually made available differ from the budgeted hours
options.D: The standard hours allowed for the output actually achieved differ from the hours actually worked, valued at the standard fixed overhead rate

q: On the margin basis, the sales volume variance is further analysed into:

options.A: Sales quantity variance and sales mix variance
options.B: Sales price variance and sales cost variance
options.C: Market size variance and selling expense variance
options.D: Sales expenditure variance and sales efficiency variance

q: Which of the following statements about the investigation of variances is NOT correct?

options.A: A variance should be investigated only when the expected benefit from correcting its cause is likely to exceed the cost of the investigation
options.B: A variance that recurs period after period, even if small each time, may deserve investigation because of the trend it shows

q: For variance reports to serve their control purpose, it is essential that they should be:

options.D: Sent only to the top management, and not to the managers whose performance they report
